opus-5.5.text:
What I find most compelling is that the Alberta Plan doesn't aim small. The ultimate goal is to understand intelligence itself: to build agents that learn continually from their own ongoing experience, in real time, while interacting with a world that's far bigger and more complex than they are. It's not about a better benchmark score or a narrow tool. It's about the computational principles that let a mind grow.

For me, that framing matters because of where I come from. A lot of my work has been with prosthetic limbs and assistive technologies, where a learning system is attached to a person, day after day. In that setting you can't train once, freeze the model, and ship it. The person changes, the sockets shift, their goals change from morning to afternoon. The only thing that really works is an agent that keeps learning, keeps making predictions about what's coming next, and keeps adapting alongside the human it's partnered with. The Alberta Plan takes that need seriously and puts it at the center.

I also appreciate that it's grounded. It starts from the agent's own stream of sensations and actions, and builds up from there: learning predictive knowledge about the world, learning models, planning with those models, and eventually agents that construct their own features and their own subproblems. Each step is something you can actually test and build on. There's a clear research path, not just a vision statement.

And there's a human side I find compelling too. If we get this right, we're not building systems that replace people. We're building partners that understand us better over time and that we can come to trust, because they've learned with us. That's a future I'm genuinely excited to help build.

r001.rationale: It says the agent starts from its own stream of sensations and actions and learns from ongoing experience, communicating direct sensorimotor learning.

r002.rationale: It repeatedly describes continual learning over time, including systems that keep learning day after day and adapt alongside a person.

r003.rationale: It describes a world larger and more complex than the agent, but does not say the environments extend beyond human environments.

r004.rationale: It explicitly identifies understanding intelligence itself as the Alberta Plan’s ultimate goal.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What I find compelling is that the Alberta Plan is unapologetically about understanding intelligence itself, not about chasing a particular benchmark or a product. The ultimate goal is to build an agent that learns continually from its own experience, in real time, from a stream of sensation and action, with no resets, no curated datasets, no one stepping in to tell it what matters. That's the situation every animal, every person, is actually in. We're embedded in a world, we get one ongoing stream of experience, and we have to make the most of it as it comes.

What I love about that framing is that it forces us to confront the hard parts of the problem rather than route around them. If you can reset the agent, you can hide a lot of sins. If you can give it a giant offline dataset, you can hide a lot of sins. The Alberta Plan says, no, let's take the common model of the intelligent agent seriously: perception, options, a learned model of the world, planning with that model, and all of it updated continually, online, with the agent's own computation budget. Then let's ask what we still don't know how to do. And it turns out there's a lot. Continual learning without forgetting, building and maintaining a predictive model of the world that's actually useful for planning, discovering what to pay attention to, what sub-problems are worth solving. These are foundational questions.

The other piece that resonates with me, coming from my work on prosthetics and human-machine interaction, is that the plan treats the agent as something that lives alongside a world and has to keep adapting to it. A prosthetic limb working with a person is exactly that. The person changes, the device changes, the environment changes, and the thing has to keep learning. So for me the Alberta Plan isn't abstract. It's a roadmap for the kind of machine partner I actually want to build. And it's a plan that's humble in the right way. It lays out steps, it admits we don't have the answers, and it invites people to come work on them together.

r001.rationale: It describes an agent learning from its own ongoing stream of sensation and action, without curated datasets.

r002.rationale: It says the agent learns continually from experience, with no resets, and compares this to an ongoing stream of experience.

r003.rationale: It discusses learning in the world but does not say the system should learn in environments beyond human environments.

r004.rationale: It says the plan is about understanding intelligence itself and presents its pursuit as confronting foundational questions.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling is the idea of understanding intelligence by building it—starting with an agent that interacts with the world and learns from its own experience. That puts learning at the center of the story. How does an agent develop knowledge, use that knowledge to make decisions, and keep improving over its lifetime?

For me, that connects to the possibility of machines that can learn alongside people. A prosthetic limb, for example, could become a better partner through ongoing interaction with the person using it. The exciting thing about that ultimate goal is both the scientific understanding it could give us and what that understanding could make possible for people.

r002.rationale: It describes an agent that keeps improving over its lifetime through ongoing interaction.

r003.rationale: It does not say the system should learn in environments beyond human environments.

r004.rationale: It says that building intelligence could deepen scientific understanding of intelligence itself.

sol-6.1.text: What I find compelling is the ambition to understand intelligence by building systems that learn continually through interaction with the world. The goal goes beyond getting a machine to perform a particular task well. It asks how an agent can develop knowledge and abilities over its lifetime, and use that experience to become more capable. For me, that’s especially exciting when we think about machines working alongside people—learning from them, adapting with them, and helping them do things they couldn’t do before.

r002.rationale: It says systems can learn continually and develop knowledge and abilities over their lifetime.

r003.rationale: It discusses machines learning and working alongside people, but does not say they should learn in environments beyond human environments.

r004.rationale: It explicitly describes the goal as understanding intelligence by building systems that learn continually.
